name: Leonardo da Vinci
excerpt: The archetypal Renaissance man, Leonardo painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper while filling thousands of notebook pages with studies of anatomy, flight, hydraulics, and optics.\n\nHe embodied the era's conviction that art and science were a single pursuit of understanding nature.

name: Nicolaus Copernicus
excerpt: A church canon and astronomer, Copernicus proposed that the Earth and planets orbit the Sun, overturning the 1,400-year-old Earth-centered cosmos of Ptolemy.\n\nPublished as he lay dying in 1543, his work opened the Scientific Revolution.

name: Galileo Galilei
excerpt: Turning the newly invented telescope to the sky, Galileo discovered the moons of Jupiter and the phases of Venus, confirming the Copernican system.\n\nHis insistence on observation over authority led to his condemnation by the Inquisition, but earned him the title of father of modern science.

name: William Shakespeare
excerpt: The most influential writer in the English language, Shakespeare wrote some 38 plays and 154 sonnets that still define tragedy, comedy, and the range of human character.\n\nWorking in Elizabethan and Jacobean London, he shaped the very vocabulary of English.

name: Johannes Kepler
excerpt: Using Tycho Brahe's meticulous observations, Kepler discovered that planets move in ellipses at varying speeds, replacing the ancient dogma of perfect circular motion.\n\nHis three laws of planetary motion gave Newton the foundation for universal gravitation.

name: Isaac Newton
excerpt: Newton's Principia unified the heavens and the Earth under three laws of motion and a single law of gravity, and he co-invented calculus to describe them.\n\nHis mechanics governed physics for two centuries and remains the language of everyday engineering.

name: Carl Linnaeus
excerpt: Linnaeus devised the binomial naming system that gives every living thing a two-part Latin name, bringing order to the chaos of natural description.\n\nHis Systema Naturae is the foundation of modern taxonomy.

name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
excerpt: A prodigy who toured Europe as a child, Mozart composed over 600 works spanning symphony, opera, and concerto with unmatched fluency.\n\nHe died at 35, leaving the Requiem unfinished and the Classical style at its height.

name: Napoleon Bonaparte
excerpt: Rising from the turmoil of the French Revolution, Napoleon crowned himself Emperor and redrew the map of Europe through a decade of conquest.\n\nDefeated at Waterloo and exiled, he left behind the Napoleonic Code that still underpins civil law across much of the world.

name: Ludwig van Beethoven
excerpt: Beethoven bridged the Classical and Romantic eras, expanding the symphony into a vehicle for personal and political expression.\n\nHe continued composing masterpieces, including the Ninth Symphony, after becoming almost completely deaf.

name: James Clerk Maxwell
excerpt: Maxwell's equations unified electricity, magnetism, and light into a single electromagnetic theory, predicting that light itself is an electromagnetic wave.\n\nHis work bridged Newton and Einstein and made radio, radar, and modern communication possible.

name: Dmitri Mendeleev
excerpt: Mendeleev arranged the known elements into the periodic table, and boldly left gaps for elements not yet discovered.\n\nWhen gallium and germanium were found with the properties he predicted, the table became one of science's great triumphs.

name: Charles Darwin
excerpt: Drawing on his voyage aboard the Beagle, Darwin argued in On the Origin of Species that life evolves through natural selection acting on inherited variation.\n\nHis theory reshaped biology and humanity's understanding of its own place in nature.

name: Abraham Lincoln
excerpt: Lincoln led the United States through its Civil War, preserving the Union and issuing the Emancipation Proclamation that set the end of slavery in motion.\n\nHe was assassinated in 1865, weeks after the Confederacy's surrender.

name: Mahatma Gandhi
excerpt: Gandhi led India's independence movement through mass nonviolent civil disobedience, from the Salt March to the campaign to quit India.\n\nHis philosophy of satyagraha inspired civil rights and freedom movements around the world.

name: Marie Curie
excerpt: Curie coined the term radioactivity and, with her husband Pierre, discovered the elements polonium and radium.\n\nShe remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, physics and chemistry, and died from the radiation she studied.

name: Winston Churchill
excerpt: As Britain's prime minister during the Second World War, Churchill's defiance and oratory rallied the nation through its darkest year against Nazi Germany.\n\nA writer and historian as well as a politician, he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953.

name: Niels Bohr
excerpt: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy fixed quantum orbits, explaining the spectrum of hydrogen and launching quantum theory.\n\nHis Copenhagen institute became the hub of twentieth-century physics, and his debates with Einstein defined how we interpret the quantum world.

name: Albert Einstein
excerpt: Einstein's theories of special and general relativity recast space, time, and gravity, while his work on the photoelectric effect helped found quantum physics.\n\nA refugee from Nazi Germany, he became the twentieth century's symbol of scientific genius.

name: Pablo Picasso
excerpt: Co-founder of Cubism, Picasso shattered the conventions of representation and reinvented his own style repeatedly across a seventy-year career.\n\nHis anti-war mural Guernica remains one of the most powerful political images in art.

name: Nelson Mandela
excerpt: Imprisoned for 27 years for resisting apartheid, Mandela emerged to negotiate its peaceful end and became South Africa's first democratically elected president.\n\nHe championed reconciliation over revenge, becoming a global symbol of moral leadership.
